title: Episode 1 (lines 155–323)
focus: Creon's first speech and the Guard

teacherSummary.text: Creon, the new king, explains to the elders that loyalty to the State comes before friendship, and that the traitor Polyneices will not be buried. A frightened Guard reports that someone has sprinkled dust on the body. Creon suspects bribery and threatens the guards.

context.history: Creon's speech echoes Athenian ideas about the city as a ship whose safety comes first. Burial "with dust" was a symbolic rite enough to satisfy the gods.

significance: Creon's reasonable-sounding principle becomes rigid. The comic Guard lowers the tension but also shows how people fear a harsh ruler.
discussionQuestions: Should loyalty to your country always come before loyalty to family?
Where does characterization appear in this scene, and what effect does it have? Point to one passage.
How does this scene connect to the book's larger concern with pride and stubbornness?

satQuestions.passage:
Elders, the gods have righted once again
Our storm-tossed ship of state, now safe in port.
But you by special summons I convened
As my most trusted councillors; first, because
I knew you loyal to Laius of old;
Again, when Oedipus restored our State,
Both while he ruled and when his rule was o’er,
Ye still were constant to the royal line.
Now that his two sons perished in one day,
Brother by brother murderously slain,
By right of kinship to the Princes dead,
I claim and hold the throne and sovereignty.

anchorPassages.note: Teaching hinge: the State as the ship that holds all fortunes; private friendship yields to public safety.
anchorPassages.text:
And I contemn the man who sets his friend
Before his country. For myself, I call
To witness Zeus, whose eyes are everywhere,
If I perceive some mischievous design
To sap the State, I will not hold my tongue;
Nor would I reckon as my private friend
A public foe, well knowing that the State
Is the good ship that holds our fortunes all:
Farewell to friendship, if she suffers wreck.

anchorPassages.note: Public law of patriotism vs outlaw: the corpse becomes the test of civic loyalty.
anchorPassages.text:
But for the miscreant exile who returned
Minded in flames and ashes to blot out
His father’s city and his father’s gods,
And glut his vengeance with his kinsmen’s blood,
Or drag them captive at his chariot wheels—
For Polyneices ’tis ordained that none
Shall give him burial or make mourn for him,
But leave his corpse unburied, to be meat
For dogs and carrion crows, a ghastly sight.
So am I purposed; never by my will
Shall miscreants take precedence of true men,
But all good patriots, alive or dead,
Shall be by me preferred and honourèd.

anchorPassages.note: Teaching hinge (dust rite): someone has given the outlaw the minimum burial the gods require.
anchorPassages.text:
Well, it must out; the corpse is buried; someone
E’en now besprinkled it with thirsty dust,
Performed the proper ritual—and was gone.
What say’st thou? Who hath dared to do this thing?
I cannot tell, for there was ne’er a trace
Of pick or mattock—hard unbroken ground,
Without a scratch or rut of chariot wheels,
No sign that human hands had been at work.
When the first sentry of the morning watch
Gave the alarm, we all were terror-stricken.
The corpse had vanished, not interred in earth,
But strewn with dust, as if by one who sought
To avert the curse that haunts the unburied dead:
Of hound or ravening jackal, not a sign.

anchorPassages.note: Tyrannical misreading: he casts piety as paid conspiracy rather than divine claim.
anchorPassages.text:
By bribes. Of evils current upon earth
The worst is money. Money ’tis that sacks
Cities, and drives men forth from hearth and home;
Warps and seduces native innocence,
And breeds a habit of dishonesty.
But they who sold themselves shall find their greed
Out-shot the mark, and rue it soon or late.
Yea, as I still revere the dread of Zeus,
By Zeus I swear, except ye find and bring
Before my presence here the very man
Who carried out this lawless burial,

literaryElements.label: Characterization
literaryElements.explanation: Creon argues like a practical ruler who puts the “good ship” of the State first; the Guard’s comic fear shows how that rigidity already frightens ordinary men.

literaryElements.label: Irony
literaryElements.explanation: Creon swears he will never shelter a public foe, while the audience knows the “foe” who has just been buried is his own niece acting from piety.

literaryElements.label: Conflict
literaryElements.explanation: The first clash is not yet Antigone versus Creon face to face, but an unseen burial against a new king’s law, reported by a terrified Guard.

themesAndDevelopment.development: Creon makes loyalty to the State outrank private friendship, while the dust on the body is already a quiet act of divine rite against that human rule.

segments.script: Creon's speech echoes Athenian ideas about the city as a ship whose safety comes first. Burial "with dust" was a symbolic rite enough to satisfy the gods. Creon's reasonable-sounding principle becomes rigid. The comic Guard lowers the tension but also shows how people fear a harsh ruler. Characterization: Creon argues like a practical ruler who puts the “good ship” of the State first; the Guard’s comic fear shows how that rigidity already frightens ordinary men. Irony: Creon swears he will never shelter a public foe, while the audience knows the “foe” who has just been buried is his own niece acting from piety. Conflict: The first clash is not yet Antigone versus Creon face to face, but an unseen burial against a new king’s law, reported by a terrified Guard. Watch for burial and the unburied body: A light covering of “thirsty dust” counts as burial, so the smallest ritual gesture is enough to break Creon’s edict and honour the gods.

segments.activity: Model the close reading of the anchor quotation using the written think-aloud below.
segments.script: First, meaning. I read “For myself, I call / To witness Zeus, whose eyes are everywhere, / If I perceive some mischievous design / To sap the State, I will not hold my tongue; / Nor would I reckon as my private friend / A public foe, well knowing that the State / Is the good ship that holds our fortunes all: / Farewell to friendship, if she suffers wreck” slowly and put it in my own words: Creon swears by Zeus that he will speak out against any plot to weaken the State, and he will not treat a public enemy as a private friend, because the State is the ship that carries everyone’s fortune. Next, craft. The ship image makes loyalty to the city sound like a rule of safety, and “Farewell to friendship, if she suffers wreck” puts the public bond above every private one. The strongest word is “ship”: it makes the State the vessel that holds every private fortune. Then, effect. What do lines 175–182 reveal about Creon's first speech and the Guard? My answer: Creon's principle sounds measured at first, but it is already rigid. The Guard's later fear in this episode shows what that rigidity does to ordinary people who serve him.
